Avalanche Bulletin


Updated on 2026-03-03 17:00:00 MST, valid until 2026-03-04 17:00:00 MST.
Valid for: Flathead-Lizard-Moyie.

    
Summary
<strong>A reactive persistent weak layer remains the primary concern for the region - especially around treeline.</strong> <strong>Retreat to more conservative terrain if you see signs of instability.</strong>

Watch for signs of instability like whumpfing, hollow sounds, shooting cracks, or recent avalanches.Start on smaller terrain features and gather information before committing to bigger terrain.Be aware of the potential for remote triggering and large avalanches due to buried surface hoar.Carefully evaluate steep lines for wind slabs.

Use appropriate sluff management techniques if the snow surface is wet.Problem 2: Wind slab.Rain on Wednesday may create potential for wet loose sluffing, especially in steep terrain. Further Detail
Avalanche Summary TuesdayThe field team felt whumpfing in the Flathead. Monday A skier triggered a size 1 persistent slab 50 cm deep. Wet loose sluffs were observed on sunny slopes. SundayExplosives triggered several persistent slab avalanches, many at treeline 40 to 70 cm deep. SaturdaySkiers remotely triggered a size 1.5 persistent slab from 30 m away while regrouping; it failed on surface hoar with a 55 cm crown depth. FridayWhumpfing & shooting cracks running 200 m were observed.
Snowpack Summary Up to 4 mm of precipitation is in the forecast for Wednesday, and may fall as rain or snow at treeline. Widespread wind effect at upper elevations left a variety of pressed surfaces, slabs, and sastrugi in open terrain. Solar-facing slopes and lower elevations likely have a surface crust. Multiple weak layers of surface hoar and/or crusts/facets may exist in the upper meter of the snowpack; the most reactive is from late January, buried 40 to 90 cm deep. Most recent persistent slab avalanches failed on this surface hoar layer in sheltered areas at treeline and below. This layer has been less reactive recently near the ski hill, but riders continue to trigger it sporadically throughout the forecast region.

title: MVP’s Mountain Weather Update
text:
Lakeman’s Lookout
The following snippet is taken from the Mountain Forecast section of FAR’s website. Bear in mind that it will be up to 24 hours old by the time you read it! Many thanks as always to Ron Lakeman for his hard work.



Mountain Weather Report


ISSUED: Tuesday March 3, 2026 11:00 MST

SYNOPSIS: A weakening frontal system will push eastward across southern BC for variable cloud/increasing cloud during the remainder of today and then occasional rain/snow (questionable snow level) tonight and early Wednesday. An upper trough will follow the cold front for a few flurries, snow showers (dropping snow level) and gusty winds Wednesday afternoon and Wednesday night.

FREEZING LEVEL: Between 1800 & 2100 metres today. Dropping to between 1400 & 1700 metres tonight. Fluctuating between 1300 & 1700 metres Wednesday. 

FERNIE ALPINE RESORT FORECAST (1615 metres):

TODAY: Cloudy with morning sunny breaks. Increasing wind during the afternoon. High 4 or 5.

TONIGHT: Cloudy with occasional rain/snow. Snow level 1600-1800 metres, dropping to between 1400 & 1700 metres overnight. Light accumulation, possible 2 to 5 cm. Windy at times. Low near 0.

WEDNESDAY: Mainly cloudy with a few flurries and afternoon snow showers, possible rain at times. Snow level 1400-1700 metres. Light accumulation, possible 3 to 8 cm. Gusty winds. High 1 or 2.

WEDNESDAY NIGHT: Mainly cloudy with a few flurries and snow showers. Light accumulation, possible 5 to 10 cm. Gusty winds during the evening. Low near -3.

OUTLOOK:

THURSDAY: Cloudy with sunny breaks. 60% chance of early morning flurries, 40% chance of afternoon flurries. Possibly windy at times. High 1 or 2. Low near -4.

FRIDAY: Cloudy with sunny breaks. Possibly windy at times. High near 4. 40% chance of flurries late Friday night. Low near 0.

SATURDAY: Mainly cloudy with a 60% chance of showers or wet flurries. Windy. High near 4. Low 0 or -1.

CONFIDENCE/DISCUSSION: Fair to good confidence of the synoptic pattern through Thursday, fair Thursday night onward. Poor to fair confidence of the snow level and the local amounts of snow tonight through Wednesday night and again Friday night and Saturday. The mild southwesterly flow makes for much uncertainty of the snow level tonight and early Wednesday. Airmass instability favours a lower snow level and is also a small risk for an isolated thunderstorm Wednesday afternoon and evening. The most recent computer models have slowed the timing of the approaching system slightly and also now suggest the following upper trough could be positioned far enough north for highly variable/locally heavy snow showers Wednesday afternoon and evening. The trend also now favours a slower passage of the trough for the possibility of a few flurries persisting into Thursday morning. A drier but unstable northwesterly flow should develop Thursday afternoon. An upper ridge of high pressure should build off the south coast Friday and Saturday, a large dissipating Pacific system could drift over it for a highly questionable chance of precipitation and equally questionable type of precipitation Friday night and Saturday.

 

Ron Lakeman.
